name: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park & Preserve
author: author-A-2026-10-08
summary:
Wrangell-St. Elias is the largest national park in the United States — the brochure counts it as six Yellowstones — a place where four mountain ranges meet and nine of the sixteen highest peaks in the country rise. Mount Wrangell still vents steam near its summit. Near the coast the Bagley Icefield, North America’s largest subpolar icefield, feeds glaciers like the Hubbard and Guyot, and the Malaspina Glacier spills out of the St. Elias Range in a mass larger than Rhode Island. Its more than 9.6 million acres of designated wilderness make up nearly a tenth of the national wilderness system, and with neighboring parks in Canada and Glacier Bay it forms a 24-million-acre World Heritage Site. [1]

This is the homeland of the Ahtna, whose territory takes in the whole Copper River Basin; some 2,500 Ahtna place names — nearly every drainage, hill and ridge named — attest to the length of their presence. Yakutat, on the coast, is a traditional Tlingit fishing village. From 1911 to 1938 the Kennecott mines near McCarthy shipped copper by rail to Cordova, and their ruins are a national historic landmark. President Carter proclaimed the area a national monument on December 1, 1978, and Congress established the 13.2-million-acre park and preserve on December 2, 1980, where local rural residents may still hunt, fish and trap for subsistence. [1] [2]

indigenous.html: The Copper River, called ’Atna’ or “beyond river” in Ahtna, runs 290 miles from the Wrangells to the Gulf of Alaska, and the Ahtna have worked and traded its copper for centuries — archeologists think for 500 to 1,000 years. In 1885 Chief Nicolai showed Lt. Henry Allen a copper vein, and later revealed a source to prospectors for a cache of supplies. Popular histories mocked him for trading a fortune for food; the historian Pratt, cited in the 2024 ethnographic overview, argues instead that he was canny and that his death around 1900 opened the way to outside exploitation. Simeone and Miller call the Kennecott mine one of the grandest colonial land thefts in early twentieth-century Alaska: the Ahtna received no compensation for the land or the ore, though they could ride the railroad free. Ahtna reaction to the 1978 monument, the authors write, was mixed: many welcomed protection for subsistence lands but felt sidelined. [2]

sources.title: Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

women.html: Two Ahtna elders, Katie John and Doris Charles, changed how Alaska’s fisheries are governed. In 1983 they and the Mentasta Village Council asked to fish at Batzulnetas, their natal village on Tanada Creek, where salmon had been taken for hundreds of years and the state had banned fishing since 1964. Refused, they sued. In March 1994 a federal court ruled that the federal government could manage subsistence fisheries on navigable waters, and the ruling was upheld in April 1995. Thousands marched in Anchorage in their support, Rosa Parks among them. John said she fought so her grandchildren would remember the way she had learned. Their victory opened Batzulnetas and extended federal subsistence jurisdiction to more than half of Alaska’s navigable waters. [2]

sources.title: Simeone & Miller, Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment (NPS, 2024)

labor_ccc.html: At Kennecott, a 14-story concentrator stepped down the hillside so gravity could carry ore through the mill. In 1916 the mines produced 101,410,000 pounds of copper — about a third of the output of the Anaconda mine in Butte with only 500 workers to Anaconda’s 15,000. The mill town was ordered by rank, the manager’s house and staff quarters at its center; the bunkhouses had no room for families, so married miners usually left theirs behind. In June 1917 miners struck — the only strike at Kennecott — for a flat wage instead of one that slid with copper prices. After 45 days of arbitration they won 50 cents a day more and new bunkhouse, mess and recreation halls, but the company refused collective contracts and rehired only one member of the Miners Committee. [3]

sources.title: Cultural Landscape Report: Kennecott Mill Town, Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve (NPS, 2001), Part I Site History

climate.html: The Tlingit named the Malaspina Glacier Sít’ Tlein, Big Glacier. At about 2,400 square kilometres it is the world’s largest piedmont glacier, and it is thinning by more than a metre a year. A 2023 radar survey found that two-thirds of it rests below sea level, cut by channels more than 350 metres deep, and that only a narrow, eroding strip of ice-cored land separates it from the Gulf of Alaska — where lagoons have formed in front of the glacier in recent decades. If the sea breaks through, the authors warn, retreat could be rapid, and the glacier holds enough ice to raise global sea level by 1.4 millimetres. [4]

World Heritage Site with Kluane, Glacier Bay and Tatshenshini-Alsek, 24 million acres; designated wilderness over 9.6 million acres, nearly 10 percent of the National Wilderness Preservation System
Ahtna homeland includes the entire Copper River Basin (~40,000 sq mi); 2,500 Ahtna place names compiled by James Kari with elders; virtually all major drainages, hills, mountains, ridges named
Yakutat is a traditional Tlingit fishing village; Copper Center, Chitina, Gulkana, Chistochina near old Athabascan settlements

Carter administration used the Antiquities Act to establish 17 monuments incl. an 11-million-acre Wrangell-St. Elias National Monument
